reference.source: Grabb & Smith's Plastic Surgery / standard references
clinicalPearls: Frostbite most often affects peripheral and exposed parts such as the fingers, toes, ears, nose, and cheeks, where tissue actually freezes, in contrast to non-freezing cold injuries
Severity is graded from superficial injury with numbness and blistering to deep injury involving muscle, tendon, and bone, though the final depth is often unclear at presentation
Frostnip is a reversible superficial cold response without ice crystal formation and resolves with rewarming, whereas true frostbite involves tissue freezing and potential necrosis
Rewarming should be rapid using a warm water bath and should only begin when there is no risk of refreezing, as refreezing dramatically worsens tissue damage
During and after rewarming the tissue is intensely painful, and adequate analgesia along with wound care and tetanus prophylaxis is important
Clear or milky blisters generally indicate more superficial injury, while haemorrhagic blisters suggest deeper damage with a worse prognosis
A conservative approach to debridement and amputation is preferred, allowing demarcation of nonviable tissue over weeks, because early appearances overestimate tissue loss

Predisposing factors include alcohol, homelessness, psychiatric illness, peripheral vascular disease, and inadequate protection at altitude, and prevention through insulation and avoiding constriction is key
reference.pathophysiology: Frostbite results from tissue freezing when heat loss exceeds the body's ability to maintain local warmth. Extracellular and then intracellular ice crystals form, causing direct mechanical cell damage and osmotic shifts. Vasoconstriction and increased blood viscosity reduce perfusion, and on rewarming there is a reperfusion phase with endothelial damage, inflammatory mediator release, microvascular thrombosis, and progressive dermal ischaemia. This secondary vascular injury and thrombosis, rather than the initial freezing alone, is responsible for much of the eventual tissue loss, which is why final demarcation takes time to declare.
additionalDifferentials: Non-freezing cold injury (trench foot / immersion foot)
Peripheral arterial occlusion or acute limb ischaemia
Cellulitis or early necrotising infection of the extremity
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of tissue viability and blister character during and after rewarming
Core temperature measurement to detect and treat associated hypothermia
Angiography or bone/technetium scanning to assess perfusion and predict tissue viability
MRI or MR angiography to help delineate viable from nonviable tissue
Inflammatory markers and wound cultures if secondary infection is suspected
redFlags: Associated systemic hypothermia requiring urgent core rewarming and resuscitation before focusing on the extremity
Deep or extensive frostbite with haemorrhagic blistering and threatened tissue loss
Signs of secondary infection, wet gangrene, or systemic sepsis
Risk of refreezing, which mandates delaying rewarming until definitively out of the cold
reference.prognosis: Superficial frostbite and frostnip usually recover fully, though long-term cold sensitivity, numbness, and neuropathic symptoms are common. Deep frostbite frequently leads to tissue loss and amputation, but because early appearance overstates the damage, delaying surgery until demarcation improves the extent of salvage. Overall outcome depends on depth, duration of exposure, refreezing, and timeliness of correct rewarming.
pitfalls: Rewarming when refreezing is still possible, which greatly worsens injury
Using dry or excessive heat, or rubbing the tissue, causing further damage
Performing early debridement or amputation before nonviable tissue has demarcated
Treating the local injury while overlooking life-threatening systemic hypothermia
Underestimating eventual tissue loss based on the early appearance
Neglecting analgesia, tetanus prophylaxis, and prevention of recurrence
management: Rapid rewarming in a warm-water bath, begun only once there is no risk of refreezing, since refreezing markedly worsens tissue loss
Concurrent treatment of any systemic hypothermia and general resuscitation before focusing on the frozen part
Adequate analgesia, typically with opioids as rewarming is intensely painful, together with tetanus prophylaxis
Prostacyclin (iloprost) vasodilator therapy and, for severe deep injury presenting within the therapeutic window, thrombolysis to salvage threatened tissue and reduce amputation
Wound care with careful blister management, elevation and treatment of secondary infection
Delaying decisions on debridement and amputation until the tissue has fully demarcated, guided by perfusion imaging
Multidisciplinary involvement of plastic surgery and rehabilitation, with counselling on long-term cold sensitivity and neuropathic symptoms
